title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 7–8 (Night 222, continuing nights-221), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 222 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Bound together in the wilderness, al-Amjad asks the old treasurer to carry two verses to the king and recites two more to his brother on the kings who went before; the treasurer weeps until his beard is wet, and al-Asʿad answers with three poems on the treachery of Time and the snares of the world. The brothers embrace, and as the treasurer raises his sword his costly horse takes fright and bolts; he throws the sword down and goes after it, and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the second and the twenty after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and twenty-second night,
sentences.n: al-thāniyatu wa-al-ʿishrūna, “the second and the twenty”: in an ordinal above twenty the unit comes first and is joined to the tens by wa-, and both parts take the case of the noun they describe, here the nominative of al-laylatu. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْأَمْجَدَ قَالَ لِلْخَازِنْدَارِ مَا نُرِيدُ مِنْكَ إِلَّا أَنْ تُبَلِّغَهُ هٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ اللَّذَيْنِ سَمِعْتَهُمَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-Amjada qāla li-al-khāzindāri mā nurīdu minka illā an tuballighahu hādhayni al-baytayni alladhayni samiʿtahumā
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that al-Amjad said to-the-treasurer: Not we-want from-you except that you-deliver-to-him these-two verses which you-have-heard-them.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that al-Amjad said to the treasurer: All we ask of you is that you carry to the king these two verses you have heard.
sentences.n: The print has ما تريد منك, a misprint for ما نريد منك, corrected here: “you do not want from you” gives no sense, and al-Amjad speaks for both brothers, as he did at the same point the night before. Shahrazād takes up the last words of the previous night. The print runs al-saʿīdu and anna together as one word, السعيدان; it is kept as set, and read as the two words al-saʿīdu anna, “fortunate, that”. anna takes its noun, al-Amjada, in the accusative. li-al-khāzindāri: li-, “to”, marks the one spoken to. mā … illā an, “we want nothing but that”, so “all we want is that”. tuballighahu hādhayni al-baytayni, “that you make these two verses reach him”: Form II ballagha takes two objects, the person (-hu, the king their father) and the thing delivered. alladhayni samiʿtahumā, “the two which you heard them”: the relative clause picks up its antecedent with the dual pronoun -humā. The shadda of تبلّغه is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَسْأَلُكَ بِاللّٰهِ أَنْ تُطَوِّلَ بَالَكَ عَلَيْنَا حَتَّى أُنْشِدَ لِأَخِي هٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ الْآخَرَيْنِ
sentences.tr: wa-asʾaluka bi-Allāhi an tuṭawwila bālaka ʿalaynā ḥattā unshida li-akhī hādhayni al-baytayni al-ākharayni
sentences.l: And-I-ask-you by-God that you-lengthen your-mind upon-us until I-recite to-my-brother these-two verses, the-other-two.
sentences.i: And I beg you by God to bear with us a little, until I have recited to my brother these two other verses.
sentences.n: asʾaluka bi-Allāhi, “I ask you by God”: bi- marks what one adjures by. ṭawwala bālahu ʿalā, literally “to lengthen one's mind upon”, is “to be patient with”: Form II of ṭ-w-l, “to make long”, and bāl, “mind”, a phrase of the everyday language; ʿalā marks the ones borne with. ḥattā with the subjunctive, unshida, “until I recite”, of something still to come; li-, “to”, marks the hearer. al-ākharayni, “the other two”, dual of ākhar, agreeing with al-baytayni. The أ of واسألك, the آ of الآخرين and the shadda of تطوّل are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَى بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا وَجَعَلَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: thumma bakā bukāʾan shadīdan wa-jaʿala yaqūlu
sentences.l: Then he-wept a-weeping intense and-set-about he-says:
sentences.i: Then he wept bitterly and began to say:
sentences.n: bukāʾan shadīdan, “a severe weeping”: the verbal noun of the verb itself, as its object and with an adjective, strengthens and colours it (the absolute object). jaʿala with an imperfect, “he set about saying”, marks the start of an action. The one weeping is al-Amjad. The ء of بكاء is printed.

sentences.t:
فِي الذَّاهِبِينَ الْاَوَّلِينَ مِنَ الْمُلُوكِ لَنَا بَصَائِرْ
كَمْ قَدْ مَضَى فِي ذَا الطَّرِيقِ مِنَ الْاَكَابِرِ وَالْاَصَاغِرْ
sentences.tr:
fī al-dhāhibīna al-awwalīna mina al-mulūki lanā baṣāʾir
kam qad maḍā fī dhā al-ṭarīqi mina al-akābiri wa-al-aṣāghir
sentences.l:
In the-gone-ones, the-first-ones, of the-kings, for-us (are) insights;
how-many have passed on this the-road, of the-great-ones and-the-small-ones!
sentences.i:
In the kings who went before us, the first to depart, there are lessons for us;
how many have passed along this road, the great and the small!
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is a short form of kāmil, two feet to the half-line, and each printed line is a whole verse whose two halves the print does not divide (they fall after al-awwalīna and after al-ṭarīqi). The rhyme is -āʾir / -āghir, the r closed by a sukūn, the pause at the end of the line: baṣāʾir, al-aṣāghir. al-dhāhibīna, “the going ones”, those who have departed, the dead. baṣāʾir, plural of baṣīra, “insight, clear proof”: lessons to see by. kam qad maḍā, “how many have passed!”: kam of wonder, with the perfect. dhā al-ṭarīqi, “this road”: dhā is the bare demonstrative, without the hā- of hādhā, a form poetry likes; the road is death. mina al-akābiri wa-al-aṣāghir: min says who the “how many” are; akābir and aṣāghir, “great ones and small ones”, plurals of akbar and aṣghar. The print writes the hamza-bearing alifs bare, الْاَوَّلِينَ, الْاَكَابِرِ, وَالْاَصَاغِرْ; the ئ of بَصَائِرْ is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْخَازِنْدَارُ مِنَ الْأَمْجَدِ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ بَكَى بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا حَتَّى بَلَّ لِحْيَتَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-khāzindāru mina al-Amjadi hādhā al-kalāma bakā bukāʾan shadīdan ḥattā balla liḥyatahu
sentences.l: And-when heard the-treasurer from al-Amjad these words, he-wept a-weeping intense until he-wetted his-beard.
sentences.i: When the treasurer heard these words from al-Amjad, he wept so bitterly that his beard was wet with tears.
sentences.n: ḥattā with the perfect, balla, “until he wet”, of a result that actually came about. balla, “to moisten”, is a doubled verb (b-l-l); the shadda of بلّ is printed. liḥya, “beard”. The ء of بكاء is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا الْأَسْعَدُ فَإِنَّهُ قَدْ تَغَرْغَرَتْ عَيْنَاهُ بِالْعَبَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā al-Asʿadu fa-innahu qad taghargharat ʿaynāhu bi-al-ʿabarāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And-as-for al-Asʿad, then-indeed-he — had-brimmed his-two-eyes with-the-tears, and-he-recited these verses:
sentences.i: As for al-Asʿad, his eyes had filled with tears, and he recited these verses:
sentences.n: wa-ammā … fa-innahu, “and as for …, (then) he”: ammā is always answered by fa-. taghargharat, from the four-letter root gh-r-gh-r (the sound of gargling), with the t- of the reflexive pattern: of eyes, “to brim with tears” that are not yet shed. It is feminine singular because it stands before its subject, ʿaynāhu, “his two eyes”, and the eye is feminine. bi-al-ʿabarāti: bi- marks what the eyes brim with; ʿabarāt is the plural of ʿabra, “a tear”. The clause rhymes al-ʿabarāt / al-abyāt.

sentences.t:
اَلدَّهْرُ يَفْجَعُ بَعْدَ الْعَيْنِ بِالْاَثَرِ * فَمَا الْبُكَاءُ عَلَى الْاَشْبَاحِ وَالصُّوَرِ
مَا لِلَّيَالِي اَقَالَ اللّٰهُ عَثْرَتَنَا * مِنَ اللَّيَالِي وَخَانَتْهَا يَدُ الْغِيَرِ
قَدْ اَضْرَمَتْ كَيْدَهَا لِابْنِ الزُّبَيْرِ وَمَا * رَعَتْ لِيَاذَتَهُ بِالْبَيْتِ وَالْحَجَرِ
وَلَيْتَهَا اِذْ فَدَتْ عَمْرًا بِخَارِجَةٍ * فَدَتْ عَلِيًّا بِمَنْ شَاءَتْ مِنَ الْبَشَرِ
sentences.tr:
al-dahru yafjaʿu baʿda al-ʿayni bi-al-athari * fa-mā al-bukāʾu ʿalā al-ashbāḥi wa-al-ṣuwari
mā li-al-layālī aqāla Allāhu ʿathratanā * mina al-layālī wa-khānathā yadu al-ghiyari
qad aḍramat kaydahā li-ibni al-Zubayri wa-mā * raʿat liyādhatahu bi-al-bayti wa-al-ḥajari
wa-laytahā idh fadat ʿAmran bi-Khārijatin * fadat ʿAliyyan bi-man shāʾat mina al-bashari
sentences.l:
Time bereaves, after the-substance, of-the-trace; * so-what (is) the-weeping over the-phantoms and-the-images?
What (is it) with-the-nights — may-release God our-stumble * from the-nights, and-may-betray-them (the) hand (of) the-changes!
They-kindled their-guile against-(the)-son (of) al-Zubayr, and-not * did-they-respect his-taking-refuge at-the-House and-the-Stone.
And-would-that-they, when they-ransomed ʿAmr with-Khārija, * had-ransomed ʿAlī with-whom they-willed of mankind.
sentences.i:
Time robs us of the trace once the thing itself is gone; * why, then, weep over phantoms and forms?
What ails the nights? May God lift us from our stumbling * at the nights' hands, and may the hand of change betray them!
They fanned their cunning into flame against Ibn al-Zubayr, and paid no regard * to his refuge at the House and the Stone.
Would that, when they ransomed ʿAmr with Khārija, * they had ransomed ʿAlī with whomever of mankind they pleased!
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is basīṭ, and the lines rhyme in -ari: bi-al-athari, al-ṣuwari, al-ghiyari, al-ḥajari, al-bashari. They lament the treachery of Time through the fall of great men of early Islam. al-ʿayn and al-athar, “the thing itself” and “its trace”: Time, having taken the person, takes even what is left of him. fajaʿa bi-, “to afflict with the loss of”: bi- marks what is lost. ashbāḥ, “phantoms, shapes”, and ṣuwar, “images”: bare outward forms. aqāla Allāhu ʿathratanā, “may God release (us from) our stumble”, is a set prayer for pardon; aqāla and khānathā are perfects used as wishes, as often in blessings and curses. al-ghiyar, “changes (of fortune)”. aḍramat, Form IV, “to kindle”; li-, “for, against”, marks the one aimed at. ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr held Mecca against the Umayyad caliphs and was killed there in 73/692, when the city was besieged, after taking refuge at the Kaʿba: al-bayt, “the House”, is the Kaʿba, and al-ḥajar, “the Stone”, the Black Stone set in it. liyādha, “taking refuge”, verbal noun of lādha bi-, “to shelter in”: bi- marks the place of refuge. raʿat, “regarded, respected”, from raʿā. The last line recalls the Khārijite plot of 40/661 to kill ʿAlī, Muʿāwiya and ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ on the same morning: ʿAmr did not come out to lead the prayer that day, and Khārija ibn Ḥudhāfa, who led it in his place, was struck down instead, while ʿAlī was killed at Kūfa. fadā X bi-Y, “to ransom X with Y”: bi- marks what is given in exchange. laytahā, “would that they”: layta takes the pronoun, the nights, as its noun. The print writes the hamza-bearing alifs bare (الْاَثَرِ, الْاَشْبَاحِ, اَقَالَ, اَضْرَمَتْ, اِذْ) and opens the poem اَلدَّهْرُ, with a fatḥa on the alif of the article; the ء of الْبُكَاءُ and شَاءَتْ is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَضَبَ خَدَّهُ بِدَمْعِهِ الْمِدْرَارِ وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذِهِ الْأَشْعَارَ
sentences.tr: thumma khaḍaba khaddahu bi-damʿihi al-midrāri wa-anshada hādhihi al-ashʿāra
sentences.l: Then he-dyed his-cheek with-his-tears the-pouring and-recited these verses:
sentences.i: Then he stained his cheek with his streaming tears and recited these verses:
sentences.n: The print has خدّة, a misprint for خدّه, corrected here. The speaker is still al-Asʿad. khaḍaba, “to dye”, as with henna; bi- marks the dye, his tears. damʿ, “tears”, a collective; al-midrār, “pouring in torrents”, the intensive pattern mifʿāl of darra, “to flow copiously”. al-ashʿār, plural of shiʿr, “poetry, verses”, takes the feminine singular demonstrative hādhihi, as non-human plurals do. The clause rhymes al-midrār / al-ashʿār. The shadda of خدّه is printed.

sentences.t:
اِنَّ اللَّيَالِي وَالْاَيَّامَ قَدْ طُبِعَتْ * عَلَى الْخِدَاعِ وَفِيهَا الْمَكْرُ وَالْحِيَلُ
سَرَابُ كُلِّ يَبَابٍ عِنْدَهَا شَنَبٌ * وَهَوْلُ كُلِّ ظَلَامٍ عِنْدَهَا كُحَلُ
ذَنْبِي اِلَى الدَّهْرِ فَلْيَكْرَهْ سَجِيَّتُهُ * ذَنْبَ الْحُسَامِ اِذَا مَا اَحْجَمَ الْبَطَلُ
sentences.tr:
inna al-layāliya wa-al-ayyāma qad ṭubiʿat * ʿalā al-khidāʿi wa-fīhā al-makru wa-al-ḥiyalu
sarābu kulli yabābin ʿindahā shanabun * wa-hawlu kulli ẓalāmin ʿindahā kuḥalu
dhanbī ilā al-dahri fa-l-yakrah sajiyyatuhu * dhanba al-ḥusāmi idhā mā aḥjama al-baṭalu
sentences.l:
Indeed the-nights and-the-days have-been-stamped * upon deceit, and-in-them (are) the-cunning and-the-tricks.
(The) mirage (of) every waste with-them (is) a-gleam-of-teeth, * and-(the)-terror (of) every darkness with-them (is) kohl.
My-sin toward Time: so-let hate its-nature * (the) sin (of) the-sword when the-hero holds-back!
sentences.i:
The nights and the days are moulded by nature * for deceit; in them are cunning and wiles.
The mirage of every waste they count a gleaming smile, * and the terror of every darkness they count kohl for the eye.
My sin against Time? Then let Time's nature condemn * the sword for its sin when the warrior holds back.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is basīṭ, and the lines rhyme in -alu: al-ḥiyalu, kuḥalu, al-baṭalu. ṭubiʿat ʿalā, “they have been stamped for”: passive of ṭabaʿa, “to stamp, impress (a nature)”; ʿalā marks the cast they were given. The print leaves the final yāʾ of اللَّيَالِي without a vowel; it is read al-layāliya, accusative as the noun of inna, which is also what the metre needs. al-ḥiyal, plural of ḥīla, “trick, ruse”. sarāb, “mirage”; yabāb, “a waste, empty land”; shanab, “the lustre and freshness of the teeth”, the beauty of a mouth. kuḥal is evidently kuḥl, “kohl”, the black powder that beautifies the eye, here with a vowel between ḥ and l that the metre requires; the form is unusual, and the print's vowel is kept; the line may intend kaḥal, the natural dark rim of the eyelids that looks like kohl. ʿindahā, “with them, in their eyes”: the nights pass off the empty mirage as a lovely smile and the dread of the dark as a beauty's kohl. dhanbī ilā al-dahri, “my sin toward Time”, is set up first as a topic; fa-l-yakrah, “then let it hate”, is li- of command with the jussive, shortened to l- after fa-. dhanba al-ḥusāmi is its object: Time might as well blame the sword when the man who holds it flinches, for the poet's “sin” is no more his own than that. idhā mā: the mā after idhā adds nothing to the sense. aḥjama, Form IV, “to hang back, flinch”. The print writes the hamza-bearing alifs bare: اِنَّ, وَالْاَيَّامَ, اِلَى, اِذَا, اَحْجَمَ.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَعَّدَ الزَّفَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma ṣaʿʿada al-zafarāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then he-sent-up the-sighs and-recited these verses:
sentences.i: Then he heaved deep sighs and recited these verses:
sentences.n: ṣaʿʿada al-zafarāti, “he sent up the sighs”: Form II of ṣ-ʿ-d, “to make rise”, as in the night before. The clause rhymes al-zafarāt / al-abyāt.

sentences.t:
يَا طَالِبَ الدُّنْيَا الدَّنِيَّةِ اِنَّهَا * شَرَكُ الرَّدَى وَقَرَارَةُ الْاَكْدَارِ
دَارٌ مَتَى مَا اَضْحَكَتْ فِي يَوْمِهَا * اَبْكَتْ غَدًا تَبًّا لَهَا مِنْ دَارِ
غَارَاتُهَا لَا تَنْقَضِي وَاَسِيرُهَا * لَا يُفْتَدَى بِجَلَائِلِ الْاَخْطَارِ
كَمْ مُزْدَهٍ بِغُرُورِهَا حَتَّى بَدَا * مُتَمَرِّدًا مُتَجَاوِزَ الْمِقْدَارِ
قَلَبَتْ لَهُ ظَهْرَ الْمِجَنِّ وَاَوْلَغَتْ * فِيهِ الْمُدَى وَتَرَتْ لِاَخْذِ الثَّارِ
وَاعْلَمْ بِاَنَّ خُطُوبَهَا تَفْجَا وَلَوْ * طَالَ الْمَدَى وَوَنَتْ سُرَى الْاَقْدَارِ
فَارْبَأْ بِعُمْرِكَ اَنْ يَمُرَّ مُضَيَّعًا * فِيهَا سُدًى مِنْ غَيْرِ مَا اسْتِظْهَارِ
وَاقْطَعْ عَلَائِقَ حُبِّهَا وَطِلَابِهَا * تَلْقَ الْهُدَى وَرَفَاهَةَ الْاَسْرَارِ
sentences.tr:
yā ṭāliba al-dunyā al-daniyyati innahā * sharaku al-radā wa-qarāratu al-akdāri
dārun matā mā aḍḥakat fī yawmihā * abkat ghadan tabban lahā min dāri
ghārātuhā lā tanqaḍī wa-asīruhā * lā yuftadā bi-jalāʾili al-akhṭāri
kam muzdahin bi-ghurūrihā ḥattā badā * mutamarridan mutajāwiza al-miqdāri
qalabat lahu ẓahra al-mijanni wa-awlaghat * fīhi al-mudā watarat li-akhdhi al-thāri
wa-iʿlam bi-anna khuṭūbahā tafjā wa-law * ṭāla al-madā wa-wanat surā al-aqdāri
fa-irbaʾ bi-ʿumrika an yamurra muḍayyaʿan * fīhā sudan min ghayri mā istiẓhāri
wa-iqṭaʿ ʿalāʾiqa ḥubbihā wa-ṭilābihā * talqa al-hudā wa-rafāhata al-asrāri
sentences.l:
O seeker (of) the-world the-base, indeed-it (is) * (the) snare (of) death and-(the)-sump (of) the-dregs;
an-abode — whenever it-makes-laugh in its-day, * it-makes-weep tomorrow: perdition to-it of an-abode!
Its-raids do-not end, and-its-captive * is-not ransomed with-(the)-greatest (of) the-stakes.
How-many a-puffed-up-one by-its-delusions, until he-appeared * rebellious, overstepping the-measure,
it-turned to-him (the) back (of) the-shield, and-made-lap * in-him the-knives, wronged-(him) for-taking the-blood-revenge!
And-know that its-calamities come-suddenly, even-if * long-is the-span and-flag (the) night-journeying (of) the-fates.
So-hold-high your-life (above) that it-pass wasted * in-it, for-nothing, without any laying-up.
And-cut (the) ties (of) love-of-it and-seeking-it; * you-will-meet the-guidance and-(the)-ease (of) the-secret-hearts.
sentences.i:
O you who seek this base world: it is * the snare of death and the sump of every trouble,
an abode that, when it brings laughter one day, * brings tears the next — perdition to such an abode!
Its raids never cease, and its captive * is not ransomed by the most precious of prizes.
How many a man, puffed up by its delusions until he showed himself * an insolent rebel who overstepped all measure,
has it turned on, showing him the back of its shield, setting its knives * to lap at him, wreaking its wrong to take its blood-revenge!
Know that its calamities come without warning, even if * the term be long and the night-march of the fates go slow.
So hold your life too dear to let it pass, squandered * in it, for nothing, with no provision laid by.
Cut the ties of love for it and of its pursuit, * and you will find guidance and ease in your inmost heart.
sentences.n: The print has مُزْدَةٍ, a misprint for مُزْدَهٍ, corrected here; the verses are otherwise pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is kāmil, and the lines rhyme in -āri: al-akdāri, dāri, al-akhṭāri, al-miqdāri, al-thāri, al-aqdāri, istiẓhāri, al-asrāri. al-daniyya, “base, low”, plays on al-dunyā, “the nearer (world)”, both from d-n-w. sharak, “snare”; al-radā, “ruin, death”; qarāra, the low ground where water settles, hence a sump; akdār, “dregs, troubles”, plural of kadar. matā mā, “whenever”, makes a condition; tabban lahā, “perdition to it!”, an accusative of cursing; min dāri, “as an abode”, min of specification. bi-jalāʾili al-akhṭāri: khaṭar is what is staked, a thing of great value, and bi- marks the price offered. muzdahin, “vain, puffed up”, is the active participle of izdahā, Form VIII of z-h-w, the t of that pattern turned to d after z; it ends like qāḍin, with the tanwīn on its last letter, and kam, “how many a”, takes it in the genitive. bi-ghurūrihā: bi- of cause, “by its delusions”. qalaba lahu ẓahra al-mijanni, “to turn the back of the shield to someone”, is an idiom for turning enemy. awlagha, Form IV of walagha, “to lap, as a dog does”: it made the knives lap his blood; al-mudā is the plural of mudya, “knife”. watarat is read as the perfect of watara, “to do someone a blood-wrong”, standing without a joining “and”; the phrase is compressed and its exact force is uncertain. al-thār is thaʾr, “blood-revenge”, printed without its hamza, and tafjā is tafjaʾu, “comes suddenly” (from fajaʾa), likewise without it; both stand as printed. iʿlam bi-anna, “know that”: ʿalima may take its clause with bi-, “know of (the fact) that”. wa-law, “even if”. wanat, “flagged”, from wanā; surā, “journeying by night”. irbaʾ bi-ʿumrika an, “hold your life above (letting it) …”, from rabaʾa bi-nafsihi ʿan, “to hold oneself above a thing”: bi- marks what is held high. sudan, “in vain”. min ghayri mā istiẓhāri, “without any provision”: mā adds “any”; istiẓhār, Form X of ẓ-h-r, “laying up a store, taking precautions”. talqa, jussive of laqiya, answers the imperative: “(and) you will meet”. rafāha, “ease, comfort”; al-asrār, “secrets”, the inmost self. The print writes the hamza-bearing alifs bare (اِنَّهَا, الْاَكْدَارِ, اَضْحَكَتْ, اَبْكَتْ and the rest); the ئ of بِجَلَائِلِ and عَلَائِقَ is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ الْأَسْعَدُ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ اعْتَنَقَ مَعَ أَخِيهِ الْأَمْجَدِ حَتَّى صَارَا كَأَنَّهُمَا شَخْصٌ وَاحِدٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha al-Asʿadu min shiʿrihi iʿtanaqa maʿa akhīhi al-Amjadi ḥattā ṣārā ka-annahumā shakhṣun wāḥidun
sentences.l: And-when finished al-Asʿad from his-verse, he-embraced with his-brother al-Amjad until they-two-became as-if-they-two (were) one person.
sentences.i: When al-Asʿad had finished his verses, he and his brother al-Amjad embraced until they were like a single person.
sentences.n: The print has شعرة, a misprint for شعره, corrected here. faragha min, “to finish”: min marks what is done with. iʿtanaqa, Form VIII, “to embrace”, takes a direct object in Classical (iʿtanaqa akhāhu, the night before); here it is joined to the brother with maʿa, “with”, for an embrace both share, a usage of the later language. ṣārā, “they two became”, dual. ka-annahumā, “as though they two”: ka-anna, “as if”, takes its noun, -humā, as a suffix, and its predicate, shakhṣun wāḥidun, in the nominative.

sentences.t: وَسَلَّ الْخَازِنْدَارُ سَيْفَهُ وَأَرَادَ أَنْ يَضْرِبَهُمَا وَإِذَا بِفَرَسِهِ جَفَلَ فِى الْبَرِّ
sentences.tr: wa-salla al-khāzindāru sayfahu wa-arāda an yaḍribahumā wa-idhā bi-farasihi jafala fī al-barri
sentences.l: And-drew the-treasurer his-sword and-wanted that he-strike-them-two, and-behold, his-horse: it-shied in the-open-country.
sentences.i: The treasurer drew his sword and was about to strike them, when all at once his horse took fright and bolted off into the wilds.
sentences.n: salla, “to draw (a sword)”, a doubled verb; the shadda of وسلّ is printed. arāda an, “he wanted to”, here “he was about to”. wa-idhā bi-farasihi, “and behold, his horse”: idhā of surprise, with bi- only marking what appears; the verb jafala then says what the horse did. jafala, “to start in fright and bolt”, of a beast. fī al-barri, “in the open country”, away into the wilds. The print spells fī with ى, فى.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ يُسَاوِي أَلْفَ دِينَارٍ وَعَلَيْهِ سَرْجٌ عَظِيمٌ يُسَاوِي جُمْلَةً مِنَ الْمَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna yusāwī alfa dīnārin wa-ʿalayhi sarjun ʿaẓīmun yusāwī jumlatan mina al-māli
sentences.l: And-it-was worth a-thousand dinars, and-on-it (was) a-saddle great worth a-sum of the-wealth.
sentences.i: It was worth a thousand dinars, and on it was a splendid saddle worth a great sum of money.
sentences.n: yusāwī, Form III of s-w-y, “to be equal to, be worth”, takes the price as a direct object. alfa dīnārin: alf takes the thing counted in the genitive singular. wa-ʿalayhi sarjun, “and on it (was) a saddle”: an indefinite subject comes after the predicate of place. jumlatan mina al-māli, “a sum of money”, here a large one; min marks what the sum is made of.

sentences.t: فَأَلْقَى السَّيْفَ مِنْ يَدِهِ وَذَهَبَ وَرَاءَ فَرَسِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-alqā al-sayfa min yadihi wa-dhahaba warāʾa farasihi
sentences.l: So-he-threw the-sword from his-hand and-went behind his-horse.
sentences.i: So he threw the sword from his hand and went after his horse.
sentences.n: The print has يدة, a misprint for يده, corrected here. alqā, Form IV of l-q-y, “to throw down”. dhahaba warāʾa, “went behind”, that is, went after it. The ء of وراء is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
